name: Hydrogen peroxide eye drops

lead: Some people have tried putting hydrogen peroxide solution in the eyes hoping to whiten or clean them. It is a household antiseptic, not an ophthalmic product.

Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising disinfectant that breaks down into water and oxygen. Contact lens systems use 3 percent peroxide with a catalytic disc that neutralises it before lenses go back in the eye. No studies support direct eye use for appearance.

paras: People who try it dilute household peroxide and drop it in the eye hoping for a cleansing effect. Contact lens peroxide systems, which are designed to be neutralised before use, are a separate product.

Reference sources state that concentrations as low as 3% can be dangerous to the eye because oxygen is released inside it. Direct eye use is associated with corneal injury. Higher concentrations cause skin burns and react violently with organic material.

angle.text: Users apply peroxide to the eye hoping it cleanses and whitens. The idea rests on anecdote, and reference sources warn that even 3 percent solution can be dangerous for the eye.

lead: Hydrogen peroxide eye drops refers to applying hydrogen peroxide solution directly to the eye, sometimes with the aim of whitening or cleansing it. It is not a medically recognised treatment for that purpose, and no published studies of it for appearance were found.

Household peroxide is typically 3 or 6 percent by weight. It is used as a surface disinfectant and, in neutralised form, for contact lens disinfection [1]. Reference sources warn that concentrations as low as 3% can be dangerous for the eye because oxygen is released within it [1].

paras: Consumer hydrogen peroxide is sold at 3 or 6 percent, with 30 percent common in laboratories and stronger grades far more hazardous [1]. Contact lenses are often disinfected in 3 percent peroxide, with a catalytic disc in the case that breaks it down before the lenses are reused [1]. Solutions up to 35 percent cause skin bubbling and pain, and concentrated solutions react violently with organic materials [1].
